method.measurement: Client latency is request start to response body end on the host. Delivery latency is response end of the write to arrival of the change frame whose transaction.request_id is the write X-Request-Id. Database counts are pg_stat_statements calls per phase (reset at phase start), classified by statement text. Memory is hmem-server VmRSS sampled once per second through docker exec; archive and large-body increments are the maximum during the event minus the maximum in the preceding 10 s. Request phases, pool counters, WebSocket and session-traffic telemetry come from the after server only; the before revision has none of them.

findings: Foreground regression: under this contention the after revision raises ordinary foreground p95 by 17.6% pooled and 2.3-3.1 times for cheap reads, and seeded capture append p95 by 49%. Its dispatcher and per-socket replay ran 7,107-7,777 outbox scans (67-74 s of statement time) and 3,169-3,405 scope locks per phase against 221-280 scans (0.9-1.2 s) and 219-319 scope locks before. Scans average about 9.5 ms; request-performance finding 3 attributes this to the replay predicate not being index-compatible. About half of the slowest 5% of after foreground time is pool wait. The extra replay work is the leading explanation consistent with these counts and waits, but it is not isolated: the before revision has no pool counters, outbox and scope-lock statement time is only 13.6-14.8% of after held connection time (79-88 s of 584-594 s), and no ablation or matched run separates the scans from other after-only changes (per-request, pool and WebSocket telemetry; 10-15 times the scope-lock calls).

Stuck catch-up and pool stripes: with ten one-connection stripes, three or four of four healthy hot-workspace sockets were retired by the 750 ms work deadline in each after run while an unrelated scope lock was held. The leading explanation is that the blocked catch-up keeps its pool connection for the whole hold, so delivery turns that need that stripe overrun the budget. The -N4 diagnostic (four multi-connection stripes) kept every healthy socket and delivered every write during the hold (p95 1.39 s), but it is one unmatched run that also cuts RTS capabilities from 24 to 4, so it is consistent with that explanation without isolating it.

Stalled observers: before, one socket that stopped reading blocked live dispatch for every client until it resumed (13-18% of hot changes delivered by phase end, 2.29 MB queued to the stalled socket). After, it was retired after about 0.3 MB and four healthy sockets received all 1,920-1,921 changes with commit-to-frame p95 0.59-0.70 s.

Snapshots: batched item writes cut insert round trips from 4,533 to 18 for 4,533 items and same-scope writer waits from 0.81-0.94 s to 0.27-0.34 s; scope-lock and page-token counts are unchanged. One before run failed a full snapshot under load with HTTP 500.

Idle: after sends no frames and runs no authorization statements while idle, but polls every retained scope once per idle sweep: 554-567 outbox scans per 30 s (5.2-5.3 s of statement time) against 240 (1.5-1.6 s) before. The cost scales with retained scope counters, not sockets. Idle transactions, including background session and archive workers, were about 125/s before (3,756-3,776 per 30 s) and 139-141/s after (4,174-4,217).
Memory: after streams archives with 49-55 MiB incremental RSS against 108-111 MiB before, and peaks 336-348 MiB under contention against 377-400 MiB before.
Telemetry: the before revision logs every WebSocket upgrade as HTTP 500; after logs them as upgrade_closed with no status and its WebSocket events agree with what clients observed.

production_rollout_decisions: Whether to deploy the change-stream delivery repairs (fbc30801) before the replay predicate is index-compatible (request-performance candidate 4). This receipt measured a foreground and capture regression for which the extra replay and polling scans are the leading, unisolated explanation; a matched rerun after that repair is required before claiming the 10% gate.

Pool striping (request-performance candidate 2) or keeping blocked database work outside delivery-turn budgets, before relying on healthy-peer progress during cold or locked catch-ups. Needs a scoped repair with a matched rerun of the stuck case on production pool settings.
Idle polling capacity: one outbox scan per retained scope per idle sweep at production scope count and outbox size (7 times this seed). Measure passively after deployment or bound it first.

OIDC grant-user audiences, TLS and reverse-proxy topologies, and production pool and RTS settings remain unqualified by this container run; confirm with passive production telemetry after any rollout.

container_cannot_satisfy: Revocation and per-user idle reauthorization: local authentication makes every principal the trusted local superadmin, so no access_revoked path or authorization query can occur in the container. Covered only by the focused grant-user specs.

Production request mix, scope count, PostgreSQL version and settings, and network path: the container is synthetic, PostgreSQL 17 with 128 MB shared buffers, plain HTTP on loopback through Docker port publishing.
limitations: Two matched runs per revision on one shared host; before-to-before pooled p95 varied by 13% (139.9 vs 123.0 ms). The most favourable pairing still regresses 9.1% pooled and every cheap read 2-3 times.
Closed-loop foreground clients: the faster before revision completed 9.2-17.6% more foreground requests in the same window. Hot writes were open-loop and matched (1,919-1,921).
No ablation or matched run isolates the explanations in the first two findings; the -N4 diagnostic changes RTS parallelism as well as pool striping.
The archive working-set gate exercised two streams of 86.4 and 34.8 MB only, not the fixed-budget 1 MiB/100 MiB/1 GiB series of the sealed-archive budgets.
Delivery latency uses the write response end; frames that arrive before the response are counted as zero or negative and are a lower bound on commit-to-visible time.
RSS sampling at 1 s does not capture continuous peaks; increments are relative to the preceding 10 s under concurrent load.

The stalled observer runs on the Docker network; the blocked catch-up holds the lock from a separate psql session for 8 s, longer than the focused spec. Admission limits (128/32) were not approached: 27 sockets shared one audience.

MCP follower diagnostics (HMEM_SESSION_TRAFFIC_DIAGNOSTICS) were not collected: capture used HTTP clients, not hmem-mcp followers. Server session_traffic warnings did not occur; every terminal proof logged verified.
The before revision has no request phases, pool counters, WebSocket or session-traffic telemetry, so those comparisons use client and pg_stat_statements measurements only.
